heroHeadline: China's Scarborough 'Marine Nature Reserve' Claim Alarms Philippine Legal Experts — Philippines DFA Files Diplomatic Protest; Reed Bank Standoff Day 3 as Xiang Yang Hong 33 Remains with CCG and 13 Maritime Militia Vessels
heroSubtitle: The Philippines faces a new institutional pressure vector at Scarborough Shoal as China declares a 'marine nature reserve' at the disputed feature (Huangyan Dao) — a move that former Supreme Court Justice Antonio Carpio warned on May 10, 2026 mirrors China's documented civilian-to-military conversion strategy at Fiery Cross Reef and Subi Reef, where weather stations and environmental facilities became missile battery sites (Philippine Daily Inquirer). The Philippine DFA filed a diplomatic protest on May 11, citing UNCLOS and the 2016 PCA ruling, which found China violated the Philippines' rights to fish at Scarborough Shoal and that no state may establish a conservation zone in contested waters excluding another state's nationals without consent. The marine nature reserve declaration is the third escalatory measure at Scarborough in five weeks — after the April 10-11 floating barrier (352 meters) and the May 9 CCG Chuanshan rights-safeguarding training — and analysts warn it could be a precursor to permanent Chinese physical construction at the lagoon entrance. Simultaneously, the Reed Bank/Iroquois Reef standoff entered Day 3, with China's research vessel Xiang Yang Hong 33 maintaining position in Philippine EEZ waters (~85 nm from Palawan) accompanied by 1 CCG vessel and ~13 maritime militia ships, as the Philippines filed a note verbale citing UNCLOS Article 246 violations for unauthorized marine scientific research. Combined with the ongoing BRP Sierra Madre garrison situation at Second Thomas Shoal, the Philippines continues to face three concurrent active SCS confrontations — an unprecedented multi-front situation that persists in the post-ASEAN Summit environment: the 48th ASEAN Leaders' Summit (Cebu, May 7-8, 2026) produced the Cebu Protocol (first ASEAN Charter amendment since 2007) and an ASEAN Leaders' Declaration on Maritime Cooperation endorsing an ASEAN Maritime Centre for the Philippines, but no binding South China Sea Code of Conduct, and China's tempo of gray zone operations has accelerated since the summit's close.
